record.paper_title: Open Problems Related to Quantum Query Complexity
record.original_question: In the glued-trees graph problem, where a quantum walk can get from the leftmost to the rightmost vertex of an exp(n)-sized graph in polynomial time with inverse-polynomial success probability while randomized algorithms need exponentially many queries to an oracle encoding the graph, does a quantum computer nevertheless need 2^Ω(n) queries to actually find a path from left to right?

evidence.quote: In 2002, Childs et al. [25] gave a celebrated quantum walk algorithm that, informally, gets from the leftmost to the rightmost vertex in the following exp ( n)-sized graph, in only poly (n) time and with 1/poly(n) success probability:
By contrast, they showed that a randomized algorithm needs 2Ω(n) queries to an oracle encoding the graph to solve the same problem (improved by Fenner and Zhang [31] to ˜Ω(2n/2)).
Problem 10 Suppose, however, that we actually want to find a path from left to right. Does even a quantum computer need 2Ω(n) queries for that task?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Define the glued-trees graph $G_n$ as follows. Take two complete binary trees of depth $n$, with roots called the entrance vertex $s$ and the exit vertex $t$, and connect their $2^n$ leaves by a random cycle that alternates between leaves of the two trees (so every leaf has degree 3 in $G_n$, while $s$ and $t$ have degree 2 and all internal tree vertices have degree 3). Vertices are labeled by random distinct strings, and the graph is presented via an adjacency-list oracle: given a vertex label, the oracle returns the labels of its neighbors. Only the labels of $s$ and $t$ are given for free; any other vertex can be probed only if its label has already been discovered through previous oracle queries.

It is known that a quantum walk algorithm can output the label of $t$, given the label of $s$, using $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ oracle queries with success probability at least $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$, while any classical randomized algorithm requires $2^{\Omega(n)}$ queries to do so.

Question: In the same oracle model, must any quantum algorithm that outputs an entire path (a sequence of labels of vertices forming a path in $G_n$) from $s$ to $t$ with probability at least $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ make $2^{\Omega(n)}$ queries to the adjacency-list oracle? Either prove such a $2^{\Omega(n)}$ quantum query lower bound, or give a quantum algorithm that finds an $s$–$t$ path using only $2^{o(n)}$ queries.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem was resolved in the negative by Jin-Peng Li, "Exponential speedup of quantum algorithms for the pathfinding problem" (arXiv:2307.12492, published 2025 in Quantum Information Processing). The work gives an efficient (polynomial-time) quantum algorithm that finds an entrance–exit path in the welded/glued-trees graph in the adjacency-list oracle model, while showing the classical task remains exponentially hard. Hence a quantum computer does not need $2^{\Omega(n)}$ queries to find a left-to-right path.

status_evidence.title: Exponential speedup of quantum algorithms for the pathfinding problem
status_evidence.snippet: We provide an efficient quantum algorithm to find an x-y path in the graph G [based on welded trees], and prove that no classical algorithm can find an x-y path in subexponential time with high probability.
status_evidence.claim: A polynomial-time quantum algorithm finds an s-t path in the glued/welded-trees graph in the adjacency-list oracle model, refuting the conjectured 2^Ω(n) quantum lower bound.

status_evidence.title: Exponential speedup of quantum algorithms for the pathfinding problem (Quantum Inf. Process., 2025)
status_evidence.snippet: An efficient quantum algorithm is provided to find an x-y path in the welded tree graph, while no classical algorithm can find such a path in subexponential time.
status_evidence.claim: Peer-reviewed publication confirming an efficient quantum pathfinding algorithm for the glued-trees problem.
